prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping, and its development to fractional uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B022 with Katori and Ye as a single part. After the first round the case rests on the same physical points: magic-wavelength trapping cancels the light shift while the lattice removes Doppler and recoil effects, so thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at once and the statistical limit changes; the result has been reproduced and exceeded at JILA, Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST with clock-to-clock agreement near 10^-18; and it has already produced physics beyond metrology, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and a many-body regime in the clock itself. That unanimity among the eight is not my reason, and I would hold the position if the count were different. In answer to the chair's wording question, I can accept 'invention and development' but I prefer that the citation name magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, because that is what separates it from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes. I would keep forward-looking phrases about dark matter or new precision tests out of the citation, since those are so far limits, not detections. Katori is credited for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for the decisive path to the record regime, and I find the two-name split defensible.
statement.case_against: The reservations are unchanged and I do not think they have been dissolved by agreement. This is a precision-measurement advance, and its largest prospective returns (dark matter, varying constants, relativistic geodesy) are still limits and consistency tests, so a reader can call it the next increment in the comb and ion-clock lineage. Credit also extends beyond two names: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Gill and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups all shaped the result, and Ye's record performance is partly a large JILA team's work. I cannot settle finer priority questions from the packet. The redefinition of the second is still pending, though I do not think it is a condition of scientific maturity.

responses.point: Pearce asks, as chair, whether a second part (B020 or B002) should share the prize and whether credit should stay limited to Katori and Ye, while stressing that B002 is a one-name credit for a large collaboration.
responses.response: I do not propose a second part. B002 still has a one-name credit for a large collaboration and source identifications at modest significance, and I defer to Mark and to astroparticle colleagues on the evidence. B020 might be defended on the ground that a quantum-simulation prize would be conceptually different from metrology, but with five candidate names and no agreed trio it would force an arbitrary exclusion, and adding it would break the three-person ceiling for the configuration. I therefore keep B022 alone and hold B020 only as a fallback.

responses.point: Kroll proposes 'invention and realisation' and accepts that the result is a measurement advance whose largest returns are prospective, and he discloses a mild personal link to the JILA community through John Hall.
responses.response: I accept 'realisation' next to 'invention' if the committee wants it, but the citation should still say how the clock works (magic-wavelength trapping) rather than only that it reaches 10^-18. On his Hall link, a disclosure by a former student in Hall's lab, with no direct tie to Katori or Ye, seems to me sufficient, since the claim is judged on reproduced results from several laboratories. I have no objection to him taking part. On the discovery-versus-tool question we agree that the answer comes from the redshift and many-body results already demonstrated.

responses.point: Lindroth resists widening the credit beyond two names but says the weighting between Katori's concept and the JILA record-setting performance has to be settled, and she wonders whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with keeping two names. The weighting is settled in practice by the citation: a clause that names the lattice concept credits Katori, and the 10^-18 development credits Ye, so a two-part wording avoids ranking one above the other. On waiting for the SI second, I would not wait. The 10^-18 agreement between independent laboratories is the maturity criterion, and the metrological decision follows from it. If Lemonde's priority is pressed, I would want primary-literature evidence of an independent magic-wavelength proposal, which none of us has produced.

responses.point: Eriksson concedes that B022 is an instrument achievement and not a new state of matter or phenomenon, and worries it sits in the same territory as the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I share the concern, but I think the separation can be argued from the physics. The comb provided the means to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock showed that a large ensemble can be interrogated without perturbation. That is a different route to the statistical limit, and it led to the gravitational-redshift and many-body results. It is still a precision advance and not a new phase, and I will not claim otherwise; the decision is whether the committee values that kind of achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation that names magic-wavelength trapping and 'invention and development', and whether members preferring 'realisation' see any difference in credit.
Whether Katori and Ye are the complete credit given Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and Gill, since I cannot verify priority from the packet.
If B022 fails to carry, whether B020 can be reduced to a defensible three-name set, and whether B043 is a better fallback in terms of credit.
statement.conflict_note: No connection from my profile bears on B022. I repeat my declared conflict on B014 (circuit QED): as a theorist in superconducting circuits, WACQT director and colleague of Chalmers groups (Delsing, Wilson), I would recuse myself from deliberation and voting on it. This has not changed. I note Kroll's disclosure on B022 and consider disclosure sufficient. WACQT's ties to Lund and KTH and Chalmers' hosting of the 2025 laureates are unrelated to B022, B020 and B043.
